subject: Heritage Studies
content: Personal identity is made up of the things that make you who you are. Key parts of identity include: your name and surname (often shows your family and clan), your totem (chidao/isiduko - shows the animal or object your clan is connected to), your religion (beliefs you follow), your nationality (the country you belong to, e.g., Zimbabwean), your home language (like Shona, Ndebele, or English), and your dress (clothes that can show your culture, like traditional attire during ceremonies). Every person's identity is a mix of their family background, culture, and personal choices.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: A totem (chidao in Shona, isithakazelo in Ndebele) is a symbol, usually an animal, that identifies a person's clan or family line. Examples of Shona totems include Shumba (Lion), Moyo (Heart), Shava/Mhofu (Eland), and Nzou (Elephant). Totems are usually inherited from the father's side of the family. Purposes of the totem system: it helps people know their clan history and ancestry, it prevents marriage between closely related people (since people with the same totem are often considered relatives and traditionally should not marry each other), it is used in totem praises (kudetemba) to show respect and honour someone, and it strengthens a sense of identity and belonging within a clan.

subject: Heritage Studies
topic: Indigenous Languages and Cultures of Zimbabwe
content: Zimbabwe officially recognizes 16 languages in its 2013 Constitution. These include Chewa, Chibarwe, English, Kalanga, Koisan, Nambya, Ndau, Ndebele, Shangani, Shona, sign language, Sotho, Tonga, Tswana, Venda, and Xhosa. Shona and Ndebele are the most widely spoken indigenous languages, while English is commonly used in government, business, and higher education. Each language group carries its own cultural practices, proverbs, and oral traditions. Recognizing many languages officially helps protect the cultural diversity and identity of all groups of people living in Zimbabwe.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: There are different types of families in Zimbabwean society. A nuclear family has parents and their children living together. An extended family includes the nuclear family plus other relatives like grandparents, aunts, uncles, and cousins, often living together or nearby and supporting each other. A polygamous family is where one parent (usually the father in traditional Zimbabwean custom) is married to more than one spouse. A child-headed family is one where a child, usually the oldest, takes on the responsibility of caring for younger siblings, often because parents have passed away or are unable to care for them. A one-parent family has only one parent raising the children. All family types can provide love, support, and guidance to their members.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: Unhu (Shona), Ubuntu (Ndebele), and Vumunhu (Tsonga) all describe the same important African value system, meaning roughly 'I am because we are' - a person's humanity is shown through how they treat others. Key attributes of Unhu/Ubuntu include: respect for elders and others, honesty, kindness and compassion, hospitality to visitors and strangers, hard work, and putting the community's wellbeing alongside your own. Common courtesies that show Unhu/Ubuntu include greeting people properly (especially elders, often with a slight bow or clapping of hands), saying please and thank you, and behaving appropriately at home, school, in the community, and at work. Someone with good Unhu/Ubuntu is described as having 'munhu' - being a good, respectful person.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: In Zimbabwean tradition, marriage is not seen as joining just two people, but two families. Indigenous marriage (kuroora in Shona, ukuthatha in Ndebele) traditionally involves the payment of 'roora' or 'lobola' (bride price) by the groom's family to the bride's family, as a sign of respect and appreciation, and to formally recognize the union between the two families. This can be paid in cattle, money, or goods, depending on agreement. Contemporary marriage types recognized in Zimbabwe today include Civil marriage (registered with the government, monogamous) and Customary marriage (following traditional practices, which historically could be polygamous). Marriage ceremonies often include family gatherings, negotiations between families, and celebrations that honour both families' heritage.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: Rules and laws exist to keep communities safe, fair, and organized. Without rules, people could not live together peacefully. In Zimbabwean tradition, disputes are resolved through a system of indigenous courts, from smallest to largest: the Village Court (headed by a village head, dara/dare, handles small disputes between neighbours or family members), the Headman's Court (handles disagreements the village head cannot resolve), and the Chief's Court (the highest traditional court, handles serious disputes and appeals). Communities, individuals, the police, and the modern court system all play roles in making sure laws are respected and followed today, working alongside these traditional structures.

subject: Heritage Studies
topic: Indigenous Political Structures: Chiefs, Headmen, and Village Heads
content: Zimbabwe has a traditional leadership structure alongside its modern government. A Chief (Ishe in Shona, Nkosi in Ndebele) leads a group of villages and is the highest traditional authority in that area, often inheriting the position and handling major community matters, land allocation, and serious disputes. A Headman leads a smaller group of villages under a chief, handling disputes too big for a village head. A Village Head (Sabhuku in Shona, Induna in Ndebele) is the leader of a single village, the first point of contact for local issues, and helps organize community activities. These traditional leaders work alongside elected local government structures like rural district councils.

subject: Heritage Studies
topic: The Early People of Zimbabwe: Khoisan and Bantu
content: The earliest known inhabitants of the area now called Zimbabwe were the Khoisan people, hunter-gatherers known for their rock art paintings found in caves and shelters across the country, some thousands of years old. Later, Bantu-speaking people migrated into the region from further north in Africa, bringing farming, iron-working, and cattle-keeping skills, and gradually became the majority population. The Bantu groups eventually developed into the Shona and Ndebele-speaking communities that make up most of Zimbabwe's population today. The contributions of these early people - farming methods, iron tools, cattle culture, and oral traditions - form an important part of Zimbabwe's heritage.

subject: Heritage Studies
topic: Pre-Colonial Kingdoms: Great Zimbabwe, Mutapa, Rozvi, and Ndebele
content: Before colonial rule, Zimbabwe was home to powerful kingdoms. The Great Zimbabwe State (about 1200-1450 AD) built the famous stone walls at Great Zimbabwe and grew wealthy through cattle and trade in gold and ivory. The Mutapa State followed, founded by Nyatsimba Mutota, ruling much of the Zambezi valley and trading with the Portuguese. The Rozvi State, led by Changamire Dombo, was known for its strong military and successfully resisted Portuguese influence. The Ndebele State was founded in the 1830s-1840s by King Mzilikazi, who led his people north from South Africa, settling in what is now Matabeleland and building a strong, organized kingdom under later King Lobengula. These kingdoms are a proud part of Zimbabwe's pre-colonial heritage.

subject: Heritage Studies
topic: Effects of First Contact with Europeans
content: From the late 1800s, Zimbabwe's first significant contact with Europeans came through three main groups: missionaries (who introduced Christianity and Western-style schools), hunters (who came seeking ivory and animal skins), and mineral prospectors (who came searching for gold and other minerals, eventually leading to colonization by the British South Africa Company under Cecil John Rhodes from 1890). This contact brought changes including new religions, new farming tools, new diseases, and eventually the loss of land and independence for local people, which later led to the liberation struggle for independence in 1980.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: Zimbabwe's national symbols represent its identity and history. The National Flag has seven stripes (green, yellow, red, black, repeated) with a white triangle and a red star with the Zimbabwe Bird in the middle. Green represents agriculture, yellow represents mineral wealth, red represents blood shed during the liberation struggle, black represents the majority population, white represents peace, and the Zimbabwe Bird is the national emblem, based on soapstone bird carvings found at Great Zimbabwe. The Coat of Arms includes two kudu antelopes, the Zimbabwe Bird, and a representation of the Great Zimbabwe walls, with the national motto 'Unity, Freedom, Work'. The National Anthem is 'Simudzai Mureza WeZimbabwe' ('Raise the Flag of Zimbabwe').

subject: Heritage Studies
content: The National Schools Pledge is recited by pupils in Zimbabwean schools, usually every morning after the National Anthem. Its wording, taken from the preamble of the 2013 Constitution, is: 'Almighty God, in whose hands our future lies, I salute the national flag. United in our diversity by our common desire for freedom, justice and equality. Respecting the brave fathers and mothers who lost lives in the Chimurenga/Umvukela and national liberation struggles. We are proud inheritors of our national resources. We are proud creators of and participants in our vibrant traditions and cultures. We commit honesty and the dignity of hard work.' Reciting the pledge is intended to build patriotism, unity, and respect for the country's history among learners.
source: ZIMSEC Heritage-Social Studies Junior Syllabus / Constitution of Zimbabwe (2013) preamble

subject: Heritage Studies
content: Zimbabwe marks several important national days each year. Independence Day (18 April) celebrates Zimbabwe's independence from British colonial rule in 1980. Africa Day (25 May) celebrates the founding of the Organisation of African Unity and African unity generally. Heroes Day (second Monday of August) honours the men and women who fought and died in the liberation struggle. Defence Forces Day (the day after Heroes Day) honours the Zimbabwe Defence Forces. Unity Day (22 December) celebrates the 1987 Unity Accord that ended conflict between ZANU and ZAPU and united the country's two main political parties. These events are usually marked with public holidays, ceremonies, and ceremonies at national shrines like the National Heroes Acre in Harare.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: Zimbabwe's natural resources are considered part of the nation's heritage, belonging to all citizens. Key natural resources include: minerals (gold, platinum, chrome, diamonds, and lithium), land (used for farming and settlement), water (rivers like the Zambezi and Limpopo, and dams like Kariba, used for drinking, irrigation, and electricity), forests and wildlife (supporting tourism and biodiversity), and wildlife reserves (home to the 'Big Five' animals, attracting visitors from around the world). Because these resources belong to the whole nation, they must be used and managed sustainably so that future generations can also benefit from them.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: Zimbabwe has three types of local government structures that manage different areas. Rural District Councils manage rural areas, including services like roads, schools, and clinics in the countryside, working alongside traditional chiefs and headmen. Urban Councils (town councils) manage smaller towns. Metropolitan/City Councils manage the largest cities, like Harare and Bulawayo, handling services such as water supply, refuse collection, road maintenance, and local by-laws. Each local government structure is led by elected councillors and a mayor (in cities) or council chairperson, who work to provide services and represent the interests of residents in their area.

subject: Heritage Studies
topic: Resolving Conflicts and Showing Good Values
content: Conflicts happen when people disagree, often because of poor communication, misunderstandings, or competing for limited resources. Zimbabwean culture values peaceful conflict resolution. In rural communities, conflicts are often resolved at the 'dare' (a traditional gathering place, often under a tree, where elders and community members discuss and settle disputes). Good values for handling conflict include: staying calm rather than fighting, listening and communicating clearly, forgiving those who have wronged you, and seeking help from a trusted elder, teacher, or the police if a conflict cannot be resolved peacefully between the people involved. As a well-known saying goes, 'a gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.'

subject: Heritage Studies
content: Zimbabwe has several important heritage sites protected as part of the nation's history. Great Zimbabwe (near Masvingo) is a UNESCO World Heritage Site famous for its ancient stone walls, built without mortar, and was the capital of a powerful pre-colonial kingdom. Khami Ruins (near Bulawayo) was the capital of the Torwa State and is also a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Matobo Hills (near Bulawayo) is known for its ancient rock art, unique granite rock formations, and spiritual significance to local communities. The National Heroes Acre (in Harare) honours liberation war heroes and other notable national figures. These sites attract tourists and help Zimbabweans and visitors learn about the country's rich history.

subject: Heritage Studies
content: Migration means moving from one place to live in another. In Zimbabwe, a common pattern is rural-to-urban migration, where people move from villages to towns and cities. Common reasons for migration include: seeking better job opportunities, access to better schools and healthcare, escaping drought or poor farming conditions, and joining family members who have already moved. Effects of migration can include overpopulation and pressure on services in towns (like housing and water), as well as fewer young people remaining in rural areas to farm. Some Zimbabweans also migrate to other countries seeking work or education, which can bring money back home (remittances) but can also mean a loss of skilled workers, sometimes called 'brain drain.'
